es.literal: to be up to the nostrils
es.meaning: To be fed up; to have had enough.
es.example: Estoy hasta las narices de sus excusas.
es.exampleTranslation: I'm fed up with his excuses.
es.regionNote: Mexico's near-equivalents: 'estar harto' is the neutral one; 'estar hasta la madre' carries the same meaning but is vulgar, not interchangeable in polite company.

it.literal: to have it up over the hair
it.example: Ne ho fin sopra i capelli di questa situazione.
it.exampleTranslation: I've had it up to here with this situation.

bridge.note: Both measure exasperation by how high it has risen — Spanish to the nose, Italian above the hair. A classic Romance mismatch: same meaning, different verb and different body part.

interference.es_to_it: Spanish builds this with estar, so Spanish speakers produce 'essere fin sopra i capelli'. Italian needs avere — and the ne, which Spanish has no equivalent for and drops almost automatically.
interference.it_to_es: Italian's avere pulls speakers toward 'tengo hasta las narices'. Spanish needs estar: estoy hasta las narices. Tener only works in the causative — 'me tienes hasta las narices', you've got me fed up. Spanish also doesn't reach for hair here; the measure is the nose.
